lines: One crate here never asks for a feature its own dependency offers.
But a sibling crate, built right alongside it, does ask for that feature. Does the first crate's own output change anyway?
answer: Cargo builds one shared copy, and a sibling's own request reaches it too.

lines: Run it for real: built alone, it prints one plain word. Built together with that sibling, the identical crate prints a different word instead, and its own source never moved.
Same two crates, but now the sibling asks for a different kind of feature, one that only adds something new instead of changing what is already there.
Does the first crate's own output change this time too?
answer: An additive feature never touches what was already there.

lines: Run it for real: alone or built together with that sibling, the identical crate prints the identical word both times.
steps.takeaway: A feature that only adds, never changes, a dependency's behavior leaves every sibling that never asked for it untouched.

lines: One crate here declares the identical dependency twice: once for its real build, and once just for its own tests, with an extra feature turned on only for those tests.
Under the resolver a modern project uses by default, does that test-only feature reach the real, non-test build anyway?
answer: The modern resolver keeps a test-only request out of the real build.

lines: Run it for real: the identical declaration, checked under the resolver an older project would default to instead, genuinely does leak into the real build. Checked under the modern resolver, it genuinely does not.
steps.takeaway: The resolver a workspace declares decides whether a dev-only feature request can reach a build nobody meant it to touch.

lines: The Cargo Book names both of these exact ideas directly, in its own words.

One line says a shared dependency is built once, with every requester's own features unified together. The other line says that is exactly why a feature should only ever add, never take away or change.
steps.takeaway: A feature's real safety is never just the crate's own property; it belongs to every combination the build can unify.

lines: So here is what this topic's own small pair of crates is really standing in for: a feature is never a private decision one crate makes alone, because the moment a sibling shares its dependency, that sibling's own request reaches you too, whether you asked for it or not.
Staying purely additive is what keeps that reach harmless instead of dangerous.
And a resolver is not just an implementation detail either, since it is the real thing deciding whether even a feature meant only for tests can quietly cross into a build nobody meant it to touch.
None of that is a matter of style. It is a matter of exactly which combinations the real build graph can actually produce.
